paras: The lynching of Dan Smith took place on December 2, 1880, at Pulaski, Tennessee, when a crowd seized Smith, a Black man, from the Giles County courtroom minutes after he was sentenced to 21 years in the penitentiary and hanged him in the bridge over Richland Creek. Smith had pleaded guilty to assaulting a white girl with intent to rape, and the papers reported that the crowd acted because the law did not allow a death sentence for the offense. The Nashville wire carried the story to dailies across the country, while Tennessee papers defended the killing and at least one Ohio paper called it murder.

Smith was accused of assaulting Mattie Hendricks, a white girl, on October 11, 1880, in the second district of Giles County. The Pulaski Citizen gave her age as thirteen, the Winchester Home Journal as ten, and the Eaton Democrat described her as an orphan. Sheriff H. Arrowsmith moved Smith to the Nashville jail, writing that he had been warned the prisoner would be taken out of the Pulaski jail that night and that he himself had been threatened with hanging.

On October 15 a meeting of South Giles residents near Thompson's mill denounced the sheriff's course and demanded Smith's return for a speedy trial, pledging not to molest him until court met. Arrowsmith promised to seek the speediest trial the law allowed. In November Judge McLemore told the grand jury that the sheriff had rescued a prisoner from a mob determined to hang him and declared that "mob-law is a remedy for nothing." The Pulaski Citizen nonetheless warned that Smith might be hanged on his arrival if punishment were delayed.

To avoid notice, Pulaski policeman Porter was made a special deputy sheriff and, with an order from Governor Marks, brought Smith from the Davidson County jail by train on December 2. The grand jury returned an indictment on two counts, assault with intent to commit rape and assault with intent to commit murder, and Smith, represented by appointed counsel Noble Smithson, pleaded guilty to both. Because the judge ruled that neither offense carried death, the jury fixed the sentence at 21 years, which the local reports called the extreme penalty of the law.

A crowd had gathered in the courtroom, and as soon as the sentence was announced it rushed the prisoner, while someone rang the courthouse bell. The Nashville wire said the mob overpowered the sheriff and posse, and the Fayetteville dispatch described a determined resistance, but the Pulaski Citizen wrote that the few officers present were unable to protect him. With a rope around his neck, Smith was led through the streets past the Presbyterian church, where the crowd briefly considered a locust tree before a voice called "On to the bridge!" Along the way his wife begged to say goodbye and was waved back.

In the covered bridge, men climbed the walls and rafters to watch as Smith was made to stand in a two-horse wagon and the rope was tied to a joist. Elder William Smith, who said he had raised both Dan and the girl, began to address the crowd until shouts of "Drive out the wagon!" cut him off. The wagon was driven out and Smith died by strangulation. The crowd's size was given as 400 in one wire version, "hundreds" in another, and 800 to 1,000 men in the Fayetteville dispatch.

After about two hours, acting coroner W. F. Alexander cut down the body and held an inquest that returned a verdict of "death by the people." No Black resident nearby would shelter the body overnight, and it was left at the colored cemetery, where Smith was buried the next morning with money the Citizen said was subscribed by the crowd that hanged him. No report of arrests, indictments or other legal action against members of the crowd appears in the coverage.

The Nashville wire of December 2 ran the next day in papers from Washington and New York to St. Paul and Chicago, under headlines such as "Bad Negro Hanged," "Condign Fate" and "Strung Up Without Warning." Shorter versions followed in weekly roundups, some of them garbled, saying Smith was hanged "while being taken to jail" or placing the lynching at "Pulaski, O."

Tennessee papers largely endorsed the killing. The Banner's Pulaski correspondent, who said he had not witnessed it, reported that no one was masked, that the crowd included "many of the best men in the county," and that everyone said amen. The Fayetteville Observer headed its dispatch "A Necksecution," and the Pulaski Citizen ran "Lynch Law!" with the deck "The People Arise in Their Wrath." The Citizen conceded that "Lynch law is not right" but held that Smith "suffered justly," and the Pulaski Herald, as quoted in Clarksville, deplored mob violence while urging that the offense be made capital.

A dissenting note came from the Jackson Standard in Ohio, which wrote that "the chivalry thought the punishment too light" and that the charge of attempted rape was treated in the South as sufficient ground for murder.

Accounts differ on the charge: the wire spoke only of assault with intent to commit murder, a Sacramento digest said "convicted of rape," and the Pulaski Citizen, the most detailed source, reported guilty pleas to both attempted rape and attempted murder. One wire version read "2 years" rather than 21, likely a dropped digit given the agreement of the other reports.

reader.title: Lynching of Dan Smith
bases: A crowd took Smith from officers in the Pulaski courtroom just after he was sentenced and hanged him from a bridge (A6, A26, A27).

Smith was hanged by a crowd variously given as hundreds or 800 to 1,000 after overpowering the sheriff and posse, and the local paper said the people meant to 'establish a tribunal of their own' because the law could not impose death for his offense (A6, A29, A25, A28).

The Nashville wire, the Banner correspondent, the Fayetteville dispatch and the Pulaski Citizen's local account independently agree on the courtroom seizure and the bridge hanging (A6, A17, A29, A26).

accounts.label: Nashville wire
accounts.gist: After a 21-year sentence for assault with intent to murder, a mob rushed the courtroom, overpowered the sheriff and posse, and with 400 or hundreds joining hanged Smith at a bridge.

accounts.label: Nashville Banner correspondent
accounts.gist: Four bell taps called the crowd, which took Smith from court to the Richmond [Richland] creek bridge; the writer did not witness it but said it was orderly, unmasked and approved by everyone.

accounts.label: Fayetteville dispatch
accounts.gist: A mob of 800 to 1,000 overpowered a resisting sheriff and posse and carried Smith down Main Street to the Richland creek bridge.

accounts.label: Pulaski Citizen local account
accounts.gist: Detailed narrative of the secret trial, the guilty pleas, the seizure from a few officers, the march past the Presbyterian church, the hanging and the inquest.

accounts.label: Roundup brief
accounts.gist: Smith was hanged by a mob while being taken to jail after arrest.

framing.detail: Northern and Western dailies ran the Nashville wire under heads such as 'Bad Negro Hanged', 'Condign Fate' and 'Strung Up Without Warning'.
The Pulaski Citizen headlined 'Lynch Law!' and 'The People Arise in Their Wrath', and concluded Smith 'suffered justly'.
The Fayetteville Observer called it 'A Necksecution' and 'The Appropriate Ending of a Lecherous Villain'.
The Pulaski Herald 'deprecate[d] and deplore[d] mob violence' but blamed the law for not making the crime capital.
The Jackson Standard (Ohio) said 'the chivalry thought the punishment too light' and mocked the attempted-rape charge as a pretext for murder.
